name: Personal Health Data Platform
tagline: A self-hosted pipeline that collects wearable data from WHOOP and Apple Health into Postgres, ready for dashboards, automations and LLMs.
problem: Wearable data is spread across vendor apps that each show their own slice of it. I wanted it all in one database I own, so I could analyse it, automate around it, and later build AI tooling on top.
architecture: Ingestion: wearable webhooks land on an edge worker that verifies each signature before anything reaches the private network. No home services are exposed to the internet.
Apple HealthKit data syncs in the background from a companion iOS app.
Processing: workflow automation reacts to ingestion events, and a Node.js service normalises sleep, recovery and workout data into Postgres.
Runs self-hosted as containerised stacks, reachable only over a private network.
Operations: TLS reverse proxy, monitoring, scheduled off-site backups, and a single alert channel. Dashboards sit on top.
outcome: A pipeline that runs without manual work, keeps every metric in one schema I control, and backs up and alerts on its own. It is the data layer for the iOS app, the MCP servers and the automations below.

diagram.footer: Ops: TLS proxy · private networking · monitoring · off-site backups · alerting

name: MCP Servers over Health Data
tagline: Secure, read-only tool access for LLMs to personal data.
problem: LLMs are most useful when they can query real data, but personal health data is exactly the kind of data you can't paste into a chat or expose broadly. The goal was to let Claude answer questions over my data without giving it write access or exposing secrets.
architecture: Postgres-backed MCP servers, one per data source.
Every request is authenticated at the edge by a zero-trust access gateway before it reaches the homelab.
The servers connect with a dedicated read-only database role. Tables holding credentials or configuration aren't granted to that role at all.
Each server offers schema search and SQL execution as tools, so the model can find the tables it needs before it queries.
outcome: Claude can answer questions like "how does my sleep change in high-strain training weeks?" directly from the source data. Database permissions enforce the access boundary, so it doesn't depend on the prompt.

name: APEX iOS App
tagline: A native Swift app for live workout heart rate from a WHOOP strap.
problem: The WHOOP app doesn't give me a live, workout-focused heart rate view or raw per-workout files. I wanted both, plus a reliable sync into Apple Health.
architecture: Connects to the WHOOP strap during workouts for live heart rate on the phone, with haptic zone alerts.
Saves each workout as a local file and uploads it to the platform backend.
Writes heart rate samples to Apple Health through HealthKit.
Dashboards read from a read-only API. Tokens live in the iOS Keychain, and there are no secrets in the code.
outcome: Live training data on my wrist and phone, with every workout archived alongside the rest of the platform's data.

name: n8n Automations
tagline: A daily morning brief of recovery and sleep, delivered to my phone.
problem: Opening three apps every morning to check recovery and sleep is friction I don't need.
architecture: A scheduled n8n workflow reads the previous night's metrics and formats them as a short brief.
The brief is delivered to a private chat, the same channel the homelab uses for alerts.
outcome: One message each morning with what matters. Next is an image-card version of the brief.

name: Truecaller CLI
tagline: A Node.js command-line tool for looking up mobile number details through Truecaller's unofficial API.
note: Uses an unofficial API. Intended for looking up your own number or numbers you're entitled to look up; respect Truecaller's terms and local privacy laws.
